extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claims for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), including determining entitlement to the benefit of an earlier filing date and assessing computer-implemented claim limitations. Uses a hypothetical facial-recognition example to teach analysis steps and examiner procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim (remember to consider whether the claims invoke 112(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet step 1. Interpret claims under their BRI and explicitly consider whether claim limitations invoke 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function). Example: determine whether terms like “capturing unit”, “analyzing unit”, etc. invoke 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze written-description support in the provisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: analyze whether each of the claim limitations has adequate written-description support in the provisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet step 2. For each limitation, ask whether the provisional specification discloses structure/material/acts sufficient to show the inventor possessed the claimed invention. Example: generic 'units' in the provisional did NOT provide sufficient detail to show possession of software/algorithmic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze written-description support in the non‑provisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: analyze whether each of the claim limitations has adequate written-description support in the non‑provisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet step 3. Evaluate whether the non‑provisional disclosure provides corresponding structure, algorithms, or other disclosure adequate to support the claim scope; if structure is present (e.g., CPU + instructions + APIDQ), written description may be adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify which features are unsupported
rubrics_metrics.description: identify which features are unsupported if support is lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet step 4. Specify which claim limitations lack adequate written-description support in either the provisional or non‑provisional disclosure and document them for potential rejections or applicant notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑prong test for applying 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means‑plus‑function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply 112(f) when claim limitations use terms that are a substitute for 'means' (generic placeholder), are modified by functional language, and are not modified by sufficiently definite structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 112(f) applies, the claim must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts described in the specification and 'equivalents thereof.' See MPEP 2181. Example: 'capturing unit', 'analyzing unit', 'determining unit', 'transmitting unit' invoked 112(f) in Original Claim 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure requirement for computer‑implemented functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer‑implemented specialized functions, the structure corresponding to the function must include a general purpose computer or computer component along with the algorithms that the computer uses to perform each claimed specialized function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A flowchart or bare functional statement is not enough; the specification must disclose sufficient algorithms/instructions. Discussion: 'the structure corresponding to the 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitations that are computer‑implemented specialized functions must include ... the algorithms that the computer uses.' If absent, limitation lacks written‑description support and may be indefinite under 112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description standard — specification must show possession
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification as filed must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule cited (e.g., Transco). Restating a function in claim language without disclosing how it is performed may fail written description, especially for software when algorithms/steps are not explained in sufficient detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be commensurate in scope with disclosed support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims cannot be broader than what the specification supports; the scope of the claim must be reasonably commensurate with the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim reciting 'at least 90% accuracy' covers up to 100% accuracy; if the specification only supports up to 97%, the claim is broader than supported and should be rejected under 112(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic placeholders vs definite structure (term‑by‑term analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether claim terms are generic placeholders invoking 112(f) or recite sufficiently definite structure that does not invoke 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'unit' used generically invoked 112(f) because it was a placeholder modified by function and lacked definite structure in the provisional; 'filter' was held to be sufficiently definite structure (one of ordinary skill would recognize 'filter' as structure) and did not invoke 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowchart/diagram disclosure may be insufficient without algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: A flowchart (e.g., Figure 2) does not necessarily provide a sufficient algorithm corresponding to claimed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a flowchart shows steps, absence of specific algorithms/implementation details can render corresponding structure insufficient for 112(f) support (not showing how to program the computer to perform specialized functions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software‑related inventions: cannot rely on supposition that one skilled could devise algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: The written‑description requirement is not satisfied merely by stating that one of ordinary skill could devise an algorithm to perform the specialized programmed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For written description, the specification must show possession (e.g., disclose the algorithm or sufficient detail), not merely assert that skilled artisans could implement it.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to question entitlement to earlier filing date / benefit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the later‑filed application is entitled to the benefit of the earlier filing date by checking whether the earlier application provides proper 112(a) support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triggering circumstances include intervening prior art, significantly broadened later‑filed claims, or when the earlier‑filed application appears substantially less than the later application. Best practice: ensure the benefit claim is proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner actions when earlier application lacks 112(a) support
rubrics_metrics.description: Notify applicant that the later application is not entitled to the earlier filing date and conduct a prior art search based on the actual filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample examiner instructions: (1) Notify applicant that claims are not entitled to benefit because earlier disclosure fails 112(a); (2) Conduct prior art search based on actual filing date and use intervening references as appropriate until benefit is shown or corrected. Suggested form paragraphs: 2.09 and 2.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for rejections and benefit denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard form paragraphs for asserting lack of entitlement or written description rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Form Paragraphs 2.09 and 2.10 for benefit-of‑earlier‑filing notice; Form Paragraphs 7.30.01 and 7.31.01 for written‑description rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Sample wording provided in workshop.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter prohibition when amending to recite specifics not in original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment that introduces a specific embodiment or species that was not present in the original disclosure may constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: adding 'Gaussian high pass filter' by amendment to a dependent claim after filing was treated as introducing new matter and not supported by original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for lack of written description: narrow claim to disclosed species
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy lack of written description for a broadly worded limitation, amend the claim to recite the disclosed species that is supported by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop example: amend to recite the disclosed APIDQ histogram technique to bring claim scope into commensuration with specification support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims do not automatically provide written‑description support
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reproducing a claim limitation in the specification, or pointing to an original claim, does not satisfy the written‑description requirement unless the claim itself conveys enough information to show possession at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is case‑by‑case and technology‑dependent; pointing to an original claim rarely suffices unless the claim conveys sufficient detail to demonstrate possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of relative terms like 'about' depends on context
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terms (e.g., 'about') are evaluated in context; they are not necessarily indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess definiteness in view of the specification, claim context, and state of the art. Example: 'about 95% accurate' did not render a claim indefinite given the relative precision available for measuring detection rates and MPEP 2173.05(B)(II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement vs written description — apply Wands factors for enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: While this workshop focuses on written description under 112(a), enablement is a related consideration and is assessed under the Wands factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion points: Given the state of the art and predictability, one skilled in the art might be able to devise programming without undue experimentation (enablement), but written description is a separate requirement. Use Wands factors when assessing enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: If 112(f) limitation lacks corresponding structure, it may be indefinite under 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the corresponding structure for a means‑style or functional limitation is not provided, the limitation can be indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) in addition to lacking written‑description support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop note: if the non‑provisional disclosure were as sparse as the provisional, 112(f) limitations would be indefinite under 112(b). See MPEP 2181 for further explanation.
